quotes.quote: Our concession agreements may be terminated at any time by the relevant governments or agencies.

fade_years.why: Ten years reflects the long but finite concession lives, with termination risk and buy-out rights held by governments.

long_run_op_margin.why: I fade to 22%, the middle of the historical 21-24% non-crisis band. Single-till and regulatory resets in Argentina, which is over half of revenue, cap upside, and the Brazil and Italy segments earn lower returns.

op_margin.why: Nine-month 2026 operating income grew slower than revenue, so the margin is down about 2.5 points. Fuel costs in Armenia, which resell at low margin, roughly doubled. I assume a modest recovery from about 22.8% in year 1 to 23.5%.

return_on_new_investment_long_run.why: The base-year return on tangible capital of 14.3% reflects old, largely amortised concession assets. New IFRIC 12 investment earns regulated, pass-through-type returns, so I use 11%, between the 8.65% break-even and 14.3%.

quotes.quote: In 2025, air traffic increased 9.8% in terms of number of passengers

rev_growth.why: Year 1 (2026) growth is high because nine-month revenue is already well above the prior year. Traffic growth, higher tariffs, Armenian fuel pass-through and construction revenue all contribute. Growth should fade toward mid-single digits as translation and inflation effects normalise.

quotes.quote: extending its term for an additional 35 years, until December 31, 2067

terminal_growth.why: Concessions run to 2038 (Argentina), 2053 (Uruguay) and 2067 (Armenia), and the cash flows are inflation-linked, so I set nominal growth slightly below the 3.75% anchor. Finite, renewable terms and emerging-market exposure justify the haircut.

risks.risk: An Argentine regulatory tariff reset or a government buy-out of AA2000 compresses margin and cash flows.
Argentine macro or FX stress cuts traffic, and a Middle East escalation lifts fuel prices and reduces demand.
Concession terms are not extended or renegotiation fails (Brazil, Neuquén, AA2000), shortening the cash flow horizon.

debt_level_representative.why: Borrowings of about 1.1bn are modest and falling, but the concession fee payable of about 1.0bn is a debt-like obligation not included in the total debt figure.

situation.margin_position: The 2025 operating margin of 24.9% sits in the middle of a 21-24% pre-COVID band. The 2023 figure of 38.6% was inflated by a one-time impairment reversal. The nine months of 2026 show a lower margin of about 23.0%, against 25.5% a year earlier, because low-margin fuel resale in Armenia and IFRIC 12 construction pass-through revenue are growing fast.

tax_rate_representative.why: The 2025 effective rate was 22.5%, but the first nine months of 2026 show income tax of 85,309 on pretax income of 309,235 (27.6%), and Argentina's statutory rate is higher.

op_margin.why: The nine-month 2026 operating margin is about 23.0%, below 25.5% a year earlier, because fuel and construction pass-through grew faster than high-margin revenue. I hold year 1 at about 22.8% (Q4 2025 was also lower) and keep roughly 22.5% thereafter.

rev_growth.why: Nine-month 2026 revenue is up 21.8%, driven by Argentina traffic and pricing, Armenia (including fuel resale) and construction revenue. Implied full-year 2026 growth is about 18%. terminal_growth.why: A USD-reporting multi-country concession portfolio with long terms (Armenia to 2067, Uruguay to 2053, AA2000 to 2038) supports growth near the long-run nominal anchor. Finite concession lives and the Argentine buy-out right argue for staying slightly below it.

Fuel-pass-through and construction mix, plus Middle East or other conflict-driven traffic and fuel shocks, keep margins near 21% instead of recovering
Argentine peso depreciation and hyperinflation, or a traffic downturn, cut USD growth sharply
Capex burden is higher than assumed (AA2000 program of about USD 7.3 billion, Florence/Pisa and Armenia plans) and returns are lower

debt_level_representative.why: Borrowings of about 1.06 billion are modest against EBITDA of roughly 0.7 billion, but the concession fee payable (about 1.05 billion, mainly Brazil) is a debt-like liability not in the reported debt.

situation.margin_position: The 2025 operating margin of 24.9% is near the 2023-2025 range outside the 2023 reversal spike, and well above the 2020-21 pandemic trough. In the first nine months of 2026 the margin fell to about 23% because low-margin jet-fuel resale in Armenia and construction-service revenue grew faster than the rest.

tax_rate_representative.why: The base-year rate of 22.5% followed a 49% charge in 2024, and the nine months to September 2026 show about 27.6% (85,309 on 309,235 pretax), so the sustainable rate is likely higher than the base year.

situation.why: 2025 operating income is sound, but below the line it holds a one-off swing in associates income (31.1m versus a 1.0m loss in 2024). Revenue is also growing far faster in 2026 (nine months +21.8%), driven partly by pass-through fuel and construction revenue at thin margins. Argentina is 54.5% of revenue and runs under hyperinflation accounting, so the reported margin depends on regulatory and FX outcomes.

business_model.claim: Corporación América Airports S.A. acquires, develops, and operates airport concessions granted by governmental authorities, operating 52 airports across Latin America, Europe, and Eurasia.
quotes: As of the date of this annual report, we operate 52 airports across Latin America, Europe, and Eurasia.
Our business consists of acquiring, developing and operating airport concessions, which are granted by governmental authorities for a limited period of time.

business_model.claim: Total consolidated revenue of 1,962.1 (table in millions of U.S.$) in 2025 consisted of Aeronautical revenue of 934.7 (47.6%), Commercial revenue of 813.1 (41.4%), Construction service revenue of 205.8 (10.5%), and Other Revenue of 8.5 (0.4%).
quotes: We classify our revenue in the following categories: (i) aeronautical revenue, (ii) commercial revenue, (iii) construction service revenue and (iv) other revenue.

business_model.claim: Aeronautical revenue comes from charging departing passenger fees, additional passenger service fees, and aircraft landing and parking fees, which are invoiced principally to airlines.
quotes: Aeronautical revenue is derived from the use of our airport facilities by aircrafts and passengers.

We charge each departing passenger a fee for the use of our airports which varies depending upon whether the passenger’s flight is an international, regional, or domestic flight, and whether the passenger is in transit or not.
These fees are invoiced to users of our airport infrastructure, principally airlines using our airports, either from their general revenue or as collected directly from airline passengers.

business_model.claim: Commercial revenue is generated from cargo warehouse usage, duty free shops, retail and food and beverage royalties and space rentals, car parking, fuel, advertising, VIP lounges, and passenger-facing services.
quotes: The majority of our commercial revenue is derived from fees resulting from warehouse usage (which includes cargo storage, storage and warehouse services and related international cargo services), services and retail stores, duty free shops, car parking facilities, catering, hangar services, food and beverage services, retail stores, including royalties collected from retailers’ revenue, and rent of space, advertising, fuel, airport counters, VIP lounges and fees collected from other miscellaneous sources, such as telecommunications, car rentals and passenger services.

business_model.claim: Under the IFRIC 12 intangible asset model, obligated airport improvements and upgrades are recognized as construction service revenue equal to costs incurred plus a reasonable margin.
quotes: We treat our investments related to improvements and upgrades to be performed in connection with our concession agreements under the intangible asset model established by IFRIC 12.
The amount of revenues for these services is equal to the amount of costs incurred plus a reasonable margin.

business_model.claim: The company’s reportable operating segments are Argentina, Italy, Brazil, Uruguay, Ecuador, and Armenia, with Argentina generating 1,069.5 (table in millions of U.S.$), or 54.5%, of 2025 total consolidated revenue.
quotes: We currently have six reportable segments: Argentina, Italy, Brazil, Uruguay, Ecuador and Armenia.

business_model.claim: Outside Argentina, 2025 consolidated revenue (table in millions of U.S.$) came from Armenia at 296.3 (15.1%), Uruguay at 192.2 (9.8%), Italy at 170.4 (8.7%), Brazil at 118.5 (6.0%), Ecuador at 114.4 (5.8%), and Unallocated at 0.7 (0.0%), while ECOGAL and Navinten are accounted for under the equity method.
quotes: Revenue and expense information on a per segment basis for Ecuador includes the results of TAGSA but does not include the results of ECOGAL.
We account for the results of operations of Navinten using the equity method.

business_model.claim: For the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026, consolidated revenue rose to 1,704,532 (table in thousands of U.S. dollars) from 1,399,522 in the prior-year period, led by Aeronautical revenue of 778,436 and Commercial revenue of 733,675.
